defaults.description.add-the-result-back-to-the-r: Add the result back to the residual stream. This preserves the original representation while letting this sublayer contribute a change.
defaults.description.the-tokenizer-breaks-text-in: The tokenizer (not shown here) has broken up the input text into pieces and assigned each piece an integer token ID. A token can be a word, or part of a word, or punctuation, or part of a Unicode character.
defaults.description.this-table-has-vocabularysiz:
This stage turns token IDs into embedding vectors in a high-dimensional vector space (dimension {embeddingDim}, for this model).  It takes a sequence of {positions} token ID integers, and turns them into a sequence of {positions} vectors, according to a lookup table learned during training. That sequence of {positions} embedding vectors will become a workspace of hidden states that passes through all the transformer blocks, getting transmuted by each one until we're ready to use it to generate the next token. We call that workspace the "residual stream."

The embedding table is just a map from token IDs to vectors, so it has {vocabularySize} token rows (the token vocabulary size plus padding), and a vector of {embeddingDim} coordinates for each token row.
defaults.note.the-break-shortens-the-token-axis-a: The break in the visualization shortens the token axis. At equal scale, this table would be {value1} times taller than wide.
defaults.description.the-selected-rows-form-the-i: The sequence of {positions} embedding vectors for the input tokens forms the initial state of the residual stream, the workspace of hidden states that passes through all the transformer blocks.
defaults.description.attention-and-feedforward-re: Attention and feedforward read from the residual stream, then add their contributions back into it. The same stream continues to the next block.
defaults.description.each-row-contains-the-vocabu: Each row contains the vocabulary scores for one sequence position. These scores are called logits. Sampling uses the final row.
defaults.description.use-the-final-position-s-log:
The sampler turns a long list of logits for the last position (position {positions}, here) into a chosen new token.

We adjust the logits using temperature (how much randomness we want) and the top-k filter, then use softmax to turn the remaining scores into probabilities. We apply the top-p filter, rescale the remaining probabilities to sum to one, and sample a token.

At temperature zero, this just reduces to choosing the token with the largest logit.
defaults.note.this-view-illustrates-the-computati: This view illustrates the computation. No prompt has been run through the model.
defaults.description.only-the-last-position-is-us: Only the last position is used to predict the next token. The generation loop also removes unused padding entries beyond the tokenizer’s vocabulary.
defaults.description.append-the-chosen-token-to-t: Append the chosen token to the context, then run the model again. This implementation recomputes the entire context on each pass; it does not use a KV cache.
defaults.description.after-the-final-transformer-:
This bit gets us from {embeddingDim}-dimensional embedding space back into a world of tokens.

After the final transformer block, RMSNorm normalizes each position’s vector. A learned matrix W then creates, for each embedding vector, a huge list of {vocabularySize} (the vocabulary size) scores which express how much the model "wants" to choose a certain token as the next token to come after that position, given knowledge only of the sequence up to that point. These scores are called logits. They are raw scores, which can be positive or negative. In practice, during inference, we only care about the last set of logits, which score the possible next tokens for the full context.
defaults.description.these-are-the-position-vecto: These are the position vectors after the final transformer block. Each row has the same sequence position it had at the input; its coordinates now contain the representation developed by all the blocks.
defaults.description.normalize-each-final-residua:
After the last transformer block, this independently normalizes each embedding vector in the residual stream.

We first scale the vector by dividing by its "Root Mean Square" (the square root of the average of the squares of each coordinate). Then we multiply each coordinate by a scale parameter (the parameter differs by coordinate, but is the same for every token position). These scale parameters are learned during training.

These normalized vectors go into the output projection, which turns them into logits.
defaults.description.final-rmsnorm-preserves-the-: Final RMSNorm preserves the number of positions and coordinates. These normalized vectors are the input to the output matrix.
defaults.description.each-of-this-matrix-s-vocabu: Each of this matrix’s {vocabularySize} rows contains {embeddingDim} learned coordinates for one vocabulary entry. Its dot product with a normalized position vector gives that entry’s logit.
defaults.note.w-is-output-layer-weight-pytorch-st: W is output_layer.weight. PyTorch stores it as vocabulary entries × residual coordinates and multiplies the normalized vectors by W.T. The break shortens the vocabulary axis.
defaults.description.each-row-contains-vocabulary: Each row contains vocabulary scores for one sequence position. Sampling uses the final row to choose the next token.
defaults.description.this-branch-normalizes-the-i: This branch normalizes the incoming residual vectors with RMSNorm, then attention mixes information across tokens and produces a contribution with the same width as the stream.
defaults.note.heads-query-heads-kvheads-key-value: {heads} query heads · {kvHeads} key/value heads · {headDim} dimensions per head
defaults.description.add-the-attention-result-to-: Add the attention result to the incoming residual stream: r₁ = r + Attention(RMSNorm(r)). The feedforward branch reads this updated r₁.
defaults.description.this-branch-reads-the-stream: This branch reads the stream after attention’s addition. RMSNorm normalizes each vector, then the feedforward network transforms it independently and produces another contribution to the stream.
defaults.description.add-the-feedforward-result-t: Add the feedforward result to the updated stream: r₂ = r₁ + FF(RMSNorm(r₁)). This r₂ becomes the next block’s incoming residual stream.
defaults.description.map-this-head-s-headdim-coor: Map this head’s {headDim}-coordinate result into a {embeddingDim}-coordinate contribution to the residual stream. Each head has its own slice of the learned output projection.
defaults.note.columns-value1-value2-of-out-proj-w: Columns {value1}–{value2} of out_proj.weight. The Python code applies all head slices together using concatenation and one matrix multiplication; this diagram shows the equivalent sum of individual contributions.
defaults.description.read-the-incoming-residual-s:
This reads the incoming residual stream and independently normalizes each embedding vector within it.

We first scale the vector by dividing by its "Root Mean Square" (the square root of the average of the squares of each coordinate). Then we multiply each coordinate by a scale parameter (the parameter differs by coordinate, but is the same for every token position). These scale parameters are learned during training.

This normalized input feeds every head in both stacks. The original residual continues to the addition along the bottom.
defaults.note.this-is-attention-norm-in-transform: This is attention_norm in TransformerBlock. It is included here as context for the attention computation.
defaults.description.head-head-computes-its-own-a: Head {head} computes its own attention pattern, then mixes the values from shared K/V pair {group}. Its result is projected separately before joining the other contributions.
defaults.note.the-bracket-marks-the-heads-using-k: The bracket marks the heads using K/V pair {group}. They share keys and values, while their queries and output-projection slices differ.
defaults.description.after-its-output-projection-: After its output projection, head {head} contributes one {embeddingDim}-coordinate vector per token. Sum these contributions across all {heads} heads, then add the total to the original residual stream.
defaults.note.the-grid-is-schematic-this-view-doe: The grid is schematic. This view does not run the prompt through the model.
defaults.description.heads-value1-use-the-same-ke: Heads {value1} use the same key and value projections. Each head still forms its own attention pattern using its own queries.
defaults.note.inspect-the-key-projection-here-or-: Inspect the key projection here, or open either head to inspect its shared key and value matrices.
defaults.description.add-the-heads-projected-cont: Add the {heads} projected contributions element by element. Every contribution has shape {td}, so their sum keeps that shape.
defaults.note.concatenate-then-project-and-projec: Concatenate-then-project and project-each-then-sum are mathematically equivalent. The code drawer shows the actual combined implementation.
defaults.description.add-the-sum-of-all-head-cont: Add the sum of all head contributions to the original residual stream. Only after this addition does the feedforward branch read the updated stream.
defaults.description.read-the-incoming-residual-s:
This reads the incoming residual stream and independently normalizes each embedding vector within it. 

We first scale the vector by dividing by its "Root Mean Square" (the square root of the average of the squares of each coordinate). Then we multiply each coordinate by a scale parameter (the parameter differs by coordinate, but is the same for every token position). These scale parameters are learned during training.

This normalized input feeds every head in the stack. The original residual continues to the addition along the bottom.
defaults.note.folding-changes-how-much-of-the-dia: Folding changes how much of the diagram is visible; it does not skip any model computation.
defaults.description.heads-range-each-contribute-: Heads {range} each contribute to the attention update. Opening another group folds this one, keeping the total diagram height fixed.
defaults.description.heads-value1-share-key-and-v:
Attention heads are divided into "groups." In each group (marked by a dotted box), the attention heads ({value1} in this case) share key and value projections.

Each head still has its own query projection and resulting attention pattern.

This is known as "grouped query attention."
defaults.note.open-either-head-to-inspect-its-sha: Open either head to inspect its shared key and value matrices.
defaults.description.head-head-computes-its-own-a: Head {head} computes its own attention pattern, then mixes the values from shared K/V pair {kvHead}. Its result is projected separately before joining all the other contributions.
defaults.note.the-dotted-box-marks-the-heads-usin: The dotted box marks the heads using K/V pair {kvHead}. Folding a group only hides its detail.
defaults.description.head-head-contributes-one-em: Head {head} contributes one {embeddingDim}-coordinate vector per token after its output projection. Sum all {heads} contributions, including those inside folded groups.
defaults.description.add-all-heads-projected-cont: Add all {heads} projected contributions, including the heads in folded groups. Each contribution has shape {td}, so their sum keeps that shape.
defaults.note.the-python-concatenates-the-head-ou: The Python code concatenates the head outputs and projects them together. This diagram shows the equivalent sum of per-head projections.
defaults.description.add-the-sum-of-all-head-cont: Add the sum of all head contributions to the original residual stream, then pass the updated stream to feedforward.
defaults.title.the-full-input-to-this-head: The full input to this head
defaults.description.this-head-reads-every-coordi: This head reads every coordinate of each normalized input vector through its learned projections.
defaults.description.multiply-the-full-input-by-t: Multiply the full input by this learned matrix to produce {value1}. {value2}
defaults.description.these-value1-depend-on-the-i: These {value1} depend on the input text. Each token has a {headDim}-dimensional vector.
defaults.note.schematic-grid-execution-playback-w: Schematic grid. Execution playback will supply activation values.
defaults.description.normalize-each-query-or-key-:
This independently normalizes each query or key vector across its {headDim} coordinates.

We first scale the vector by dividing by its "Root Mean Square" (the square root of the average of the squares of each coordinate). Then we multiply each coordinate by a scale parameter learned during training.

Query and key normalization have separate sets of {headDim} scale parameters. Each set is shared across token positions and heads. The normalized queries and keys then go into RoPE. Values are not normalized here.
defaults.description.rotate-pairs-of-query-or-key: Rotate pairs of query or key coordinates by an angle determined by token position. This gives the attention scores information about relative positions.
defaults.description.compare-every-query-with-eve: Compare every query with every key. Each dot stands for a dot-product score, before masking or scaling. Q and K here include normalization and RoPE.
defaults.note.the-raised-t-means-transpose-dot-si: The raised T means transpose. Dot sizes are illustrative; they do not show measured scores or their signs.
defaults.title.hide-future-tokens: Causal mask to hide future tokens
defaults.description.replace-scores-above-the-dia: Replace scores above the diagonal with negative infinity: column > row means a future token. Leave the diagonal and all earlier positions available. Scaling preserves negative infinity, and softmax gives the masked future positions exactly zero weight.
defaults.description.the-upper-triangle-contains-: The upper triangle contains −∞ wherever the key is later than the query. The lower triangle, including the diagonal, keeps the original raw scores. The next step scales these scores and applies softmax.
defaults.note.the-mask-pattern-is-exact-for-this-: The mask pattern is exact for this context length. Dots retain the same illustrative sizes as the corresponding unmasked scores.
defaults.description.divide-the-masked-scores-by-: Divide the masked scores by √{headDim}, then apply softmax across each row. The positive divisor keeps masked entries at negative infinity; softmax turns them into zero. The remaining weights sum to one.
defaults.note.moving-this-division-after-the-mask: Moving this division after the −∞ mask gives the same attention weights as scaling before masking.
defaults.description.each-row-tells-a-query-how-m: Each row tells a query how much to read from each value vector. Zeros exclude future tokens. The dots stand for input-dependent mixing coefficients, and each row sums to one. The first row is exactly [1, 0, …].
defaults.note.dot-sizes-are-illustrative-the-0-1-: Dot sizes are illustrative. The 0/1 entries follow exactly from the causal mask. Attention weights are activations computed from the input.
defaults.description.multiply-the-attention-weigh: Multiply the attention-weight matrix by V. Every output row is a weighted sum of the allowed value vectors. The result has one row per token and one column per head coordinate.
defaults.note.one-mixed-value-vector-per-token-th: One mixed value vector per token. The next step, shown one level up, projects this head’s output into a contribution to the residual stream.
defaults.description.use-the-query-at-position-ro: This score is the dot product of the query vector at position {row} from head {head}, and the key vector at position {column} from shared K/V head {kvHead}. Both vectors have already passed through their Q/K normalization and RoPE.
defaults.note.the-grid-shows-symbolic-activations: The grid shows symbolic activations after Q/K normalization and RoPE.
defaults.description.every-row-is-a-normalized-an: Every row is a normalized and rotated query vector from head {head}. Row {row} is the query vector for sequence position {row}.
defaults.description.transpose-turns-each-key-row: Transpose turns each key row into a column. Column {column} contains k from shared K/V head {kvHead}, after normalization and RoPE.
defaults.description.read-the-residual-stream-aft:
This reads the residual stream after attention’s contribution has been added and independently normalizes each embedding vector within it.

We first scale the vector by dividing by its "Root Mean Square" (the square root of the average of the squares of each coordinate). Then we multiply each coordinate by a scale parameter (the parameter differs by coordinate, but is the same for every token position). These scale parameters are learned during training.

This normalized input feeds both the gate and value projections. The unnormalized stream continues to the addition along the bottom.
defaults.description.each-row-is-the-current-repr: Each row is the current representation at a sequence position, after the attention contribution and feedforward normalization. The same learned matrices act independently on every row.
defaults.description.expand-each-row-into-the-int: Expand each row into the intermediate dimension, using the same learned matrix at every position. This path will become the gate after a SiLU activation.
defaults.description.a-second-learned-projection-: A second learned projection expands each input row. The gate modulates this path element by element.
defaults.description.silu-multiplies-each-value-b: SiLU is a nonlinear activation function that multiplies each value by its sigmoid: x × sigmoid(x). This produces a smooth activation "gate" for the neural network, including small negative values.
defaults.description.multiply-the-silu-gate-and-t: At each sequence position in isolation, multiply the outputs of the SiLU gate path and the value path, coordinate by coordinate.
defaults.description.project-each-gated-row-back-: Project each gated row back to the residual-stream width, using one shared learned matrix. Its result is then added to the incoming residual at the same position.
defaults.title.a-contribution-to-the-residual-str: A contribution to the residual stream
defaults.description.each-output-row-is-added-to-: Each output row is added to the residual stream at the corresponding sequence position. The output has the same shape as the input.
defaults.description.add-each-feedforward-output-: Add each feedforward output row to the corresponding row of the stream after attention: r₂ = r₁ + FF(RMSNorm(r₁)).
defaults.description.this-branch-reads-the-residu:
Feedforward is essentially a traditional neural network that operates independently to transform each embedding vector in our sequence. Each line through the diagram represents one embedding vector in our sequence of {positions}. There is no mixing across the sequence positions; that happens only in attention.

It contains three Linear layers (Gate, Value, and Down Projection), and sprinkles of nonlinear magic in the form of the SiLU activation function, and the multiplication between the gate and value branches.

Feedforward normalizes the input, projects each vector *up* into a larger {expandedDim}-dimensional vector space, operates on it there, and then projects it back down into our familiar {embeddingDim}-dimensional embedding space. As with attention, the result is then added back into the residual stream running through all the transformer blocks.
defaults.title.generating-the-next-token: A big box of math for generating a new token from a context
defaults.description.the-whole-context-travels-th:
At a high level, the LLM is a big box of math (mostly matrix multiplications) performed in order, from left to right in our diagram. Our mathematical machine takes in a token sequence (the context) and spits out a new token. We append that token to the context, and repeat to generate another new token.

At this top level, we can break the machine out into three stages:

1. Input machinery, which embeds each token in the input sequence in a high-dimensional vector space ("embedding vectors")
2. A *lot* of stacked transformer blocks. We pass the embedding vector sequence through these blocks, and they operate on the vectors in the sequence until the last embedding vector position contains the information used to generate the next token.
3. Some output machinery which turns the embedding vectors back into a weighted list of possible tokens, and which then chooses ("samples") one token from that list.
defaults.description.attention-lets-tokens-exchan:
A transformer block has two components: the Attention mechanism and Feedforward. Both are branches from the residual stream that take in the embedding vector sequence from the stream, operate on it, and add the result of those operations back into the stream. Following [The Transformer Circuits Paper](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2021/framework/index.html), we can see the stream as an information "bus" that runs all the way through the transformer blocks from end to end.

Attention and Feedforward differ in how they operate on the sequence of vectors in embedding space. Remember, for a sequence of {positions} input tokens, we have a sequence of {positions} vectors each of dimension {embeddingDim}. Attention is structured to allow exchanges of information *between* the {positions} vectors; informally, it "mixes meaning" between words/tokens/vectors at different positions in the sequence. Feedforward does not mix across positions. It transforms the vector at each position independently, with no information exchanged between the {positions} vectors.
defaults.description.every-head-reads-the-same-no:
Every attention head does a series of mathematically identical operations but with different learned weights; it represents a different way of doing attention that is learned at training time.

This is "Grouped-Query Attention", meaning each head has its own Query projection, but heads are formed into groups that share K and V projections. For an explanation of Q, K and V, and a visualization of how the attention math works, click on a specific attention head to zoom.

The contributions of all the heads are summed back into the residual stream.
defaults.note.heads-query-heads-kvheads-k-v-pairs: {heads} query heads / {kvHeads} K,V pairs / {headDim} dimensions per head
defaults.description.taking-dot-products-of-query:
Now we come to the heart of the machine, the attention mechanism. If you haven't encountered attention before, be warned: this section needs a *lot* more information to actually *explain* the attention mechanism. Alas, this margin is too narrow to contain it. Apologies, dear reader; soon, I will post something longer elsewhere.

The tldr, though, is that all this linear algebra allows information to be exchanged *across* embedding vector sequence positions, according to a mathematical recipe that is *learnable* by the model during training (it learns the weights in the W_q, W_k, W_v matrices). 

W_q, W_k, and W_v act on the input embedding vectors to produce "query", "key", and "value" vectors in a smaller {headDim}-dimensional vector space. After that, we apply a normalization and then RoPE (Rotary Positional Encoding) to the query and key vectors. RoPE adds positional information by rotating these vectors, allowing the model to "know" their relative positions in the sequence when computing attention between a pair of vectors.

Taking dot products of query and key vectors then produces the attention scores, in a {positions}x{positions} matrix. After masking, scaling, and softmax, the resulting weights are then used in a weighted sum of the value vectors.

If you zoom up one level, you'll see that a final output transformation is then applied to get the output of the attention head in the original embedding space, and outputs of all the heads are combined with a sum.

The mask exists to enforce *causality* in the sequence, by preventing earlier vector positions from drawing information from later positions.

If you understand all of that, you probably already learned attention someplace else. Soon, I'll post that longer tutorial for people who are coming to this most interesting part of the LLM internals for the first time.
defaults.note.uses-k-v-pair-kvhead-all-heads-are-: Uses K,V pair {kvHead}. All heads are computed together in Python.
defaults.description.two-learned-projections-expa: Two learned projections expand the current vector at each sequence position. A nonlinear gate modulates one path, and a final projection returns it to the residual width. Every row uses the same learned matrices.
defaults.note.position-value1-is-sequence-index-v: Position {value1} is sequence index {value2} in Python. Token IDs and learned-weight row numbers keep their original values.
defaults.description.token-id-value1-selects-row-: Token ID {value1} selects row {value2} of the embedding table. Its {embeddingDim} coordinates form this token’s starting vector.
defaults.label.last-position-only:
sample at the
last position only
defaults.label.append-to-the-context-then-take-an: Append the new token to the context, then make another forward pass through the model for another new token
defaults.label.read-the-residual-normalize-once-a: Read the residual, normalize once, and share that input with every head.
defaults.label.each-w-slice-maps-headdim-embeddin: Each Wₒ slice maps {headDim} → {embeddingDim}. Click a head to open it; click its matrix to see real weights.
defaults.label.all-heads-share-the-input-unfold-a: All heads share the same input. You can unfold folded groups to inspect their heads.
defaults.label.visible-of-heads-heads-unfolded-al: {visible} of {heads} heads shown unfolded (all {heads} still contribute)
defaults.label.rows-query-positions-columns-key-p: Rows = query positions · columns = key positions
defaults.label.v-carries-the-information-to-read-: V carries the information to read from each token
defaults.label.w-learned-matrices-q-k-v-input-dep: W = learned matrices    ·    Q, K, V = input-dependent activations
defaults.label.q-and-k-here-are-after-normalizati: Q and K here are after normalization and RoPE.
defaults.label.the-vector-width-expands-and-contr: The vector width expands and contracts while the number of positions stays the same.
defaults.caption.feedforward-diagram:
Each line represents one embedding vector.
The vectors at each position in the sequence are transformed __independently__ by feedforward.
There is no mixing across the sequence positions; that happens only in attention.
defaults.caption.score-diagram:
Row {row} of the Q matrix is the *q* ("query") vector for sequence position {row},
and column {column} of the Kᵀ matrix is the *k* ("key") vector for sequence position {column}.
Their dot product *q* · *k* is one attention score at position ({row}, {column}) in the attention matrix.
defaults.caption.model: Token embeddings pass through the transformer blocks. The final position’s output scores are used to choose the next token, which is appended to the context.
defaults.caption.output: Final RMSNorm normalizes each position vector, then the learned output matrix maps it to vocabulary scores. The same normalization and matrix are applied at every sequence position. Sampling uses the final row of logits.
defaults.caption.block: Attention combines information from each position and the positions before it. Feedforward then transforms each position independently. Both results are added to the residual stream.
defaults.caption.attention: Each head combines value vectors using its own attention weights. Its output projection maps the result to the residual width; summing these contributions gives the attention update. Heads in a dotted box share keys and values.
defaults.caption.head: Query–key dot products give attention scores. Masking, scaling, and softmax turn those scores into attention weights, which determine how the value vectors are combined at each position.
defaults.caption.feedforward: The same learned projections transform each position independently. SiLU turns one expanded path into a gate, which multiplies the other path coordinate by coordinate; the down projection returns it to the residual width.
defaults.caption.feedforward-residual: The feedforward branch reads the stream after attention’s addition. RMSNorm normalizes each position vector, then the gate, value, and down projections transform it independently. The result is added back at the same position.
defaults.caption.score: Score ({row}, {column}) is the dot product of row {row} of Q and column {column} of Kᵀ. Each vector has {headDim} coordinates.
defaults.caption.attention-two-stacks: Each head combines value vectors using its own attention weights. Its output projection maps the result to the residual width; summing these contributions gives the attention update. Heads in a bracket share keys and values.
defaults.page.title: LLMs under the hood
defaults.page.introduction:
Hi! I'm [Nadia Wadzinski](http://www.nadiawadzinski.com/), and this is the annotated LLM architecture visualization tool I [built](note:page.build-note) for my own use. Perhaps it will be useful to you, too. I hope it's interesting not just to people professionally interested in LLM internals, but also to anyone who gets joy from opening up complex machinery to see how it works inside.
**To start, try clicking on one of the transformer blocks to zoom in, then keep zooming into the attention heads, as far as you can go!**
The model is [Qwen3 0.6B (dense)](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/model_doc/qwen3). It came out in April 2025, ancient history in LLM years. Nonetheless, I like using it as my [model organism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Model_organism) for LLMs. It's a scrappy little reasoning model that you can run on a MacBook Air, and a good jumping-off point to understand more sophisticated LLM architectures. And you can implement it in just 145 lines of PyTorch, excluding the tokenizer and sampler. You can open up that code below to see it alongside the model, and you can also jump to the code for different parts of the model by clicking on the [code] icons. NB: we're not actually running the model here; the attention scores and next token are illustrative.
I've shown the model without a KV cache, to make it as simple as possible. Soon, I'll add a KV cache toggle to the visualization, along with a viz of Qwen3 mixture-of-experts and more recent model architectures (Qwen3.8-27B!). The emphasis on showing the residual stream flowing through the model end to end owes a lot to Anthropic's [Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2021/framework/index.html) paper from 2021.
Finally: it may occur to you after exploring this annotated visualization for a while that understanding the mathematics of the LLM architecture does not actually tell you a whole lot about [how LLMs work at a deeper level](note:page.interpretability-note), or why they are able to do the things they do. The truth is that an LLM architecture is really just a series of empty mathematical boxes, with recipes for how information flows between them. These boxes provide a structure in which we *grow* all the organic complexity of the LLM weights during training. But that's a discussion for another time.
defaults.legend.title: Legend
defaults.legend.note: Matrix sizes are schematic. See the labels for actual dimensions.
defaults.legend.operation: An operation or a whole block
defaults.note.illustrative-continuation: Illustrative continuation: “ end” is one token and “.” is another, produced on the following pass. This example has not been run through the model.
defaults.note.future-score: This key is in the future. The dot product is computed, but the causal mask later replaces it with −∞, giving it zero attention weight.
defaults.note.allowed-score: This key is at or before the query position, so the causal mask will preserve this score. Scaling and softmax come later.
defaults.note.feedforward-rows: The row numbers identify sequence positions. The vectors contain the representations developed so far in this block and the preceding blocks.
defaults.explanation.notation: The visualization numbers token positions starting at 1; Python indexes the sequence starting at 0. {positions} Block and head numbers, token IDs, and weight coordinates match the code.
defaults.explanation.weight-storage: Estimated weight tensor data only. Activations and runtime overhead take up additional memory.
defaults.page.build-note:
Yes, the visualizations in this tool were (of course) created using a coding agent, though with a pretty firm hand on the tiller from me and many many rounds of prompting to get what I had in mind. I have strong opinions about some of this stuff, and you get results proportionate to the effort and intention you put in, with these things.

It should be pretty obvious, but I wrote the important annotations myself. (There may be occasional LLM-generated text in some of the smaller and less, ahem, *load-bearing* captions.) I can't write CSS to save my life, but prose is another matter. And writing about something always helps me learn it better; "writing is thinking", as the saying goes. Furthermore, I think the best teaching material should come with a strong authorial voice so that you feel the presence of the person behind it, a human being who walked the same learning path as you, who wrestled with the material, and who wrestles with it still.
defaults.page.interpretability-note: If you're interested in this topic, you'll probably want to read some [Mechanistic Interpretability research](https://www.anthropic.com/research/team/interpretability), which aims to understand not just the architecture but also the emergent mechanisms that live inside the actual numbers in LLMs (e.g. in the trained weights, activations, etc.).
